content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has emphasized the importance of reducing the time between HIV diagnosis and the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). This involves integrating and linking services, such as offering CD4 cell count testing at the point of care. The WHO guidelines on HIV testing services highlight best practices to improve linkage to care, derived from published studies and programmatic experiences. These practices align with new recommendations to enhance the transition from testing to care and ART initiation. The costs of specific interventions vary depending on their components and the context of implementation. However, no studies in the systematic review provided direct cost or cost-effectiveness estimates. Effective linkage to HIV care after diagnosis can improve program outcomes, support earlier ART initiation, and reduce loss to follow-up, potentially leading to cost savings across the care continuum. Qualitative evidence synthesis identified key interventions to support linkage to care, such as counseling and support from healthcare workers and case managers, as well as family and peer support. Service delivery interventions include home-based HIV testing and ART initiation, integrated services at single facilities, same-day CD4 cell count testing, transportation assistance, decentralized ART provision, and community-based ART distribution. Trained lay providers, peer navigators, and community outreach workers play a critical role in supporting patients and addressing loss to follow-up. Communication technologies, such as mobile phones and text messaging, can aid in disclosure, adherence, and retention, particularly for adolescents and young people. Strengths-based case management and partner testing are also effective strategies. HIV programs must address barriers to care and ART initiation, especially for populations facing structural and individual challenges. For children, poor linkage and retention remain issues, particularly for infants tested through early infant diagnosis (EID) programs. Family-centered service delivery models and point-of-care technologies for infant HIV diagnosis are recommended. Adolescents face unique challenges, including developmental changes, limited health awareness, and consent requirements. Peer support groups, community-based services, and mobile technology interventions can improve linkage to care for this age group. CD4 cell count testing at the point of care is recommended to prioritize patients for urgent linkage to care and ART initiation. While ART initiation for all people living with HIV regardless of CD4 count is the ultimate goal, many regions still face delays in diagnosis and care linkage. Point-of-care CD4 testing can reduce turnaround times and improve access to clinical monitoring. Studies have shown that point-of-care CD4 testing is cost-effective, even in low-income settings, due to its health benefits in reducing morbidity and mortality. Electronic communication systems, such as SMS/GSM/GPRS printers, can reduce delays in acting on laboratory results, particularly for early infant HIV diagnosis. These systems have been implemented in several countries, reducing turnaround times and improving access to results in rural settings. While formal cost-effectiveness analyses are lacking, the health benefits of earlier identification of HIV-positive infants likely offset the intervention costs. Further research is needed to assess the clinical impact of these technologies on ART initiation rates, loss to follow-up, and infant mortality and morbidity. HIV programs should retain the capacity for baseline CD4 cell count testing and monitoring treatment failure, as CD4 count remains a key predictor of disease progression and mortality risk. Point-of-care instruments should be strategically placed based on factors such as patient volume, distance, and cost. Integration of point-of-care programs into existing laboratory and clinical systems is essential to ensure synergy and strengthen linkage to care and treatment. In summary, the WHO guidelines advocate for a comprehensive approach to improving linkage to care, emphasizing the importance of timely ART initiation, cost-effectiveness, equity, and acceptability. Further research is needed to evaluate the impact of these strategies and technologies on clinical outcomes and program effectiveness.
